summary: Describes how other ARPANET sites could submit batch jobs to the University of California, Santa Barbara computer and fetch the printed results. A program called RJE listened at a published socket, and users needed an account at the UCSB computer center. It is a site-specific service description from 1971, not a general protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: You hand a big stack of work to a faraway computer by mail, and later it mails back the answers. This note explains the exact way to address the envelope for the computer at Santa Barbara.

questions: how did ucsb remote job entry work
how to submit batch jobs over the early arpanet
subtitle: How ARPANET users could submit batch jobs to a UCSB mainframe and fetch the printed output.

tldr.problem: Network users needed exact instructions for sending batch jobs to the University of California, Santa Barbara 360/75 and retrieving results.
tldr.mechanism: A process called RJE at socket x'200' accepts card-image files in three input classes, and a process called RJOR at socket x'300' returns job output using a flag byte, an 8-byte job name and op-coded records.
tldr.outcome: It is a site-specific service description from 1971 and was updated by RFC 217.

today: The unit metadata lists the status as unknown, and the RFC was updated by RFC 217. The text describes a service at one site, not a general protocol.

sections.title: Remote Job Entry at UCSB
sections.content:
UCSB accepted pseudo card files for batch processing at socket number x'200', site 3. Users needed an account number from the UCSB Computer Center, and account #1025 with programmer names such as UCLA, SRI or UTAH could be used during checkout. The 360/75 ran OS MVT and HASP, and an intermediary process called RJE handed jobs to HASP.

A user logs in by opening a simplex connection to socket x'200' through the Logger. RJE serves one user at a time and the NCP queues other requests. It drops a connection if it waits more than one minute per record, and it treats the user closing the connection as end of file.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one mail slot for jobs. Only one person can use it at a time, and the others wait in line.

sections.title: The Three Input Classes
sections.content:
RFC 105 says RJE expects a first byte of zeros (message Type 0) and ignores IMP-message boundaries afterwards. The second byte declares the input class: 00 is Class A (stream-oriented), 10 is Class B (variable-length record) and 11 is Class C (fixed-length record), and the declaration holds for the life of the connection.

Whatever the class, the file is sent as card images padded or truncated to 80 bytes, structured as if put on the card reader. Jobs needing special disks or tapes need a /*SETUP card after the job card. In Class A the third byte is a break character that ends each card image. In Class B each record is a one-byte op code x'01', a two-byte length in bits (a multiple of 8) and the text. In Class C the file is simply a string of 80-byte card images.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the computer three ways how your cards are packed: separated by a special mark, each with a length label, or all exactly the same size.

sections.title: Retrieving Output with RJOR
sections.content:
Class A SYSOUT output could be fetched from socket x'300', site 3, if the character T was the eighth positional accounting parameter on the job card. A process called RJOR answers there. The user sends an Input Connection message with a flag byte and an 8-byte EBCDIC job name, then RJOR closes it and replies over a second connection from its socket x'301' to the user's socket one less than the one used for contact.

The flag bits are: bit 0 transmit output, bit 1 purge output, bit 2 wait as long as needed, and bit 3 cancel an earlier wait request. RJOR's reply is the job name followed by logical records, each with a one-byte op code, a two-byte length and text. Op code x'01' carries one output record, and the other defined op codes, 00 to 0B, report events such as end of file, purged output, I/O errors and waiting for output.
sections.plainLanguage: To get your answers back you hand over a slip with the job name and what you want. The computer then sends the printout, or a note explaining why it cannot yet.
